metadata.name: [Audit] Successful sign-in after failed sign-ins
metadata.description: Five or more failed sign-ins, then a successful sign-in within 30 minutes, for the same account name or from the same public address. Elastic's internal network addresses never count as the same address. Kibana does not record failed sign-ins, so the failures are always Elasticsearch's, but the successful sign-in can be to Elasticsearch or to Kibana. Start on Identity & Access with the address in Client IP, then check each identity that signed in on Identity 360.

query.base: SET unmapped_fields="nullify"; FROM logs-elastic_cloud.serverless_audit.otel-default | WHERE @timestamp <= ?_tend AND @timestamp > ?_tstart | WHERE event.action IN ("authentication_failed","anonymous_access_denied", "authentication_success", "user_login") | STATS n = COUNT(*), first_ts = MIN(@timestamp), last_ts = MAX(@timestamp), early = TOP(@timestamp, 5, "asc") BY user.email, api_key.name, user.domain, user.name, failed_signin = COALESCE(event.action IN ("authentication_failed","anonymous_access_denied"), false), client.ip | EVAL match = ["same account", "same address"] | MV_EXPAND match | EVAL match_value = CASE(match == "same account" AND NOT user.name IN ("elastic.maintenance","autoscaling","elasticsearch-controller","elastic/fleet-server","elastic/kibana", "(unattributed)","<anonymous>","<unauthenticated-cloud-access-token>","<unauthenticated-saml-user>","<unauthenticated-cloud-api-key>"), user.name, match == "same address" AND NOT CIDR_MATCH(client.ip, "100.64.0.0/10"), TO_STRING(client.ip)) | WHERE match_value IS NOT NULL | INLINE STATS failures = SUM(n) WHERE failed_signin, first_fail = MIN(first_ts) WHERE failed_signin, fails = TOP(early, 5, "asc") WHERE failed_signin BY match, match_value | WHERE failures >= 5 AND (failed_signin OR last_ts > MV_MAX(fails)) | EVAL actor = CASE(user.email IS NOT NULL, user.email, api_key.name IS NOT NULL, api_key.name, user.domain == "_cloud_api_key", CONCAT(user.name, " · Cloud API key"), user.domain == "_es_api_key", CONCAT("Unnamed key of ", user.name), user.name IS NOT NULL, user.name, "(unattributed)") | EVAL identity_kind = CASE(user.email IS NOT NULL, "Person", api_key.name IS NOT NULL, "Elasticsearch API key", user.domain == "_es_api_key", "Unnamed API key", user.domain == "_cloud_api_key", "Cloud API key", user.domain == "_service_account", "Service account", failed_signin, "Failed sign-in", user.name IS NULL, "Unattributed", "Other") | STATS failures = MAX(failures), first_fail = MAX(first_fail), last_success = MAX(last_ts) WHERE NOT failed_signin, failed_names = VALUES(actor) WHERE failed_signin, failed_from = VALUES(client.ip) WHERE failed_signin, signed_in = VALUES(actor) WHERE NOT failed_signin, signed_in_types = VALUES(identity_kind) WHERE NOT failed_signin, successes = SUM(n) WHERE NOT failed_signin BY match, match_value | WHERE last_success IS NOT NULL | EVAL severity = CASE(match == "same account", "high", "medium") | KEEP severity, match, match_value, failed_from, failed_names, signed_in, signed_in_types, failures, successes, first_fail, last_success

data.content:
**What it means.** Someone failed to sign in five or more times, and within 30 minutes a sign-in succeeded, either as the same account name or from the same public address. "Same account" means a guessed name got in: treat it as urgent. "Same address" means the address that was failing also had a successful sign-in. That is often your own office, VPN or shared network, where a script has a wrong password while everyone else signs in normally.

**Triage**
1. Open **[Audit] 🔐 Identity & Access** with the time range from the alert's first failure to its last success. Set **Client IP** to the address (for a same-account alert, to each address the failures came from).
2. In **Failed sign-ins and denied access** and **Top failed or denied access**, see which names were tried and how fast. Generic names (admin, elastic, root) or many different names point to guessing; one name failing again and again points to a stale password in a script.
3. Open **[Audit] 👤 Identity 360** and pick each identity that signed in, in the **Identity** dropdown. Check **Who this is — by identity and principal id**, **Busiest addresses they used** and **Where they connected from**: is this address normal for them?
4. On the same page, read **⚠️ What they changed — deletes first, then newest** and **What they read, by index family**. Anything after the sign-in that this identity does not usually do is the reason to act.
5. If the sign-in is not explained, revoke the API key or end the person's sessions, rotate the credential, and block the address.

**What is normal.** Your own offices, VPNs and automation hosts fire the "same address" form when a scheduled job keeps a wrong password while people sign in successfully. If the address is yours and the failed names belong to a known script, fix the script. Elastic's internal network addresses never count as the same address.
